briefs.headline: Sebi to issue guidelines for usage of AI in markets: Pandey
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Sebi will soon issue detailed guidelines for the responsible use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the capital markets, its chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said, emphasising the need to balance technological innovation with investor protection.
The Sebi chief said the proposed guidelines would focus on establishing appropriate guardrails for AI use, including disclosures, accountability of regulated entities and a 'human-in-the-loop' approach to ensure that critical decisions are subject to human oversight.
In June 2025, Sebi floated a consultation paper proposing guiding principles for responsible usage of Artificial Intelligence (AI)/Machine Learning (ML) applications/models in securities markets.
These guiding principles are intended to optimise benefits and minimise potential risks associated with the integration of AI/ML based applications in securities markets to safeguard investor protection, market integrity, and financial stability.
Speaking at the inauguration of Sebi's pavilion at the 45th India International Trade Fair 2026, Pandey said the regulator has been continuously strengthening its cybersecurity framework to address rising cyber threats.
He highlighted growing concerns over cyberattacks targeting financial institutions and cryptocurrency platforms, as well as digital frauds involving social media influencers. Following emerging threats, the regulator also introduced a structured incident response mechanism in May this year, aligned with the Financial Stability Board's FIRE reporting template, he said.

briefs.headline: Indian liqueur companies carve out space with new flavours
briefs.bodyText:
BENGALURU: Indian liqueur makers are looking beyond conventional flavours and imported labels to carve out a space alongside global names such as Kahlua, Baileys and Tia Maria. From spice-led liqueurs and traditional herbal infusions to coffee blends, they are turning local flavours into contemporary drinks, hoping to build curiosity and repeat purchases.
Rajasthan's heritage liqueur maker Maharani Mahansar draws on recipes from Mahansar's erstwhile royal family. MD Surendra Pratap Singh traces his family's tradition to 1768. The family resumed commercial production in 2005. Ingredients include Pushkar roses, Kerala cardamom and oranges from Nagpur.
He says the country liquor tag makes Indians associate traditional drinks with cheap alcohol. "We have always felt our own things were inferior," he said. Younger buyers and women are changing his business. Rose has overtaken fennel, accounting for 50-60% of sales. He put FY26 turnover at Rs 80 crore.
Palasa, a cream liqueur, launched in Delhi late October. Former market researcher Lekshmi Krishnan developed its Indian blend of saffron, rose, cardamom, nuts and fruit. 
It is mixed with Dutch cream and bottled in the Netherlands.
She says "these are all ingredients that, you know, we all know and love."
Goa-based Quaffine began commercial operations in September 2022. Co-founder Olson Pereira, a former bartender, drew on Chennai's filter coffee for the cold-brew liqueur. The recipe took about 11 months to develop during the pandemic. He sees specialty coffee culture and espresso martinis helping create demand. 
"Our tutor is Instagram today," he said, describing how consumers discover cocktails.
Bandarful, a cold-brew coffee liqueur launched in 2024 by Uttarakhand's Himmaleh Spirits, uses Chikmagalur beans and Himalayan spring water. It sells in Delhi, Haryana, Uttarakhand and Goa. "We believe the origin adds to the appeal, but ultimately, the taste has to deliver," the company said.
Familiar ingredients can resonate at home while offering "a touch of the exotic for international audience," said Vikram Achanta, co-founder of beverage consultancy Tulleeho. There is a practical opening, too. Pereira recalls switching between imported coffee liqueurs because "the supply was inconsistent." Achanta says that dependable availability lets bars commit to cocktails using a particular brand.

briefs.headline: After MNCs, domestic companies embrace GCC model
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Global capability centres (GCCs), initially set up by MNCs in India to tap skilled talent, lower operating costs and manage global operations more efficiently, are finding growing acceptance among Indian businesses too. From conglomerates to companies with overseas operations, domestic firms are creating dedicated centres to bring technology, finance and human resources under one roof, reflecting a shift towards centralised operations.
Top conglomerates including Adani, Tata and Mahindra, have adopted the model to integrate operations, standardise processes and drive digitisation across their businesses.
For better efficiency
While no specific number capturing the rising trend is available yet, multiple companies and industry experts confirmed to TOI that adoption is gathering pace across sectors.
India has 2,117 GCCs employing around 2.36 million professionals, according to the Nasscom-Zinnov FY26 report. Most are MNC-led, with mandates extending beyond cost arbitrage to technology, AI, engineering and product development.
Says Bhanu Prakash Kalmath SJ, healthcare industry leader, Grant Thornton Bharat: As businesses become more global, digitally intensive and organisationally complex, dedicated capability centres can give strategic leverage and consolidate functions otherwise dispersed across business units or external providers, while building common technology platforms, retaining institutional knowledge, strengthening innovation and creating deeper pools of specialist talent, while delivering efficiency''.
Indian conglomerates, which have global operations have also been adopting the model to drive up efficiency and competitive advantage, adds Shalini Pillay, India leader - GCC, KPMG India. The trend is also spread to mid-sized companies with service providers helping them to establish and scale such centres.
Some groups are taking this a step further by commercialising capabilities developed for captive internal use. For instance, Strides Pharma's Arcolab, which began as a captive shared-services organisation, evolved into Pivot Path recently.
Companies such as ITC, Tata Steel and the JSW Group have captive shared-services centres supporting their wider businesses. Separately, ITC Infotech has set up a Future Capability Centre for a UK-based client, and is helping other companies establish GCCs.
Further, the pharmaceutical sector has adopted the trend, particularly among domestic companies with sizeable international operations. Domestic companies are increasingly exploring the GCC model to achieve scale and tap into innovation, taking a cue from MNCs that have expanded their GCC operations, said Sujay Shetty, global health industries advisory leader, PwC India.

briefs.headline: Food items see price escalation
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Resurgence in the price of food items like rice, pulses, vegetables, sugar, fruits, coarse grains and protein rich items like meat and fish is bound to impact the living costs for households. Far from a localised blip in inflation, a TOI analysis of NSO data reveals a sweeping price escalation across the nearly 200-odd food items ledger.D
Households which saw price relief earlier this year are now essentially facing a U-turn as prices for both the staples and other daily use items continue to rise, as headline retail inflation touched 6.09% in Oct, crossing RBI's 6% red line for the first time under the new base series, driven by a widespread firestorm in the food basket which had pushed food inflation to 8.9% in the month.
Data shows prices of staple rice (12.5%), millets (38%), jowar (18.7%) and vegetables such as onions (116%), garlic (60%) and ginger (48%) have swung vigorously by Oct from a contraction zone recorded earlier this year. Pulses like arhar (15%), urad (11.6%), gram (7.4%) and fruits such as banana (11%), papaya (15%), lemon (48%), apple (18%) and litchi (17%) also mirror this swing.
Households getting hit
Protein-rich food items such as chicken (11.3%) and egg (8.3%) saw slight price deceleration in Oct, yet remained high. 
Buffalo meat (15.3%) and fish (8.5%) prices accelerated further during the month. Cooking mediums which include edible oils such as refined oil (16%), groundnut oil (16.5%), and mustard oil (9.8%), along with spices - dry chillies (23%), coriander (22%) and turmeric (8%) also felt the price pinch.
Domestic cost-of-living squeeze is bleeding into the broader macro economy, with dining out becoming significantly more expensive as restaurants and accommodation services inflation jumped to 10% in Oct, driven by a price rise in cooked snacks and limited-service cafes. Transport costs ticked further during the month, on the back of surging domestic airfares (43.2%) and steady inflation in petrol (7.5%) and diesel (8.4%) prices.

briefs.headline: Loan repayment cap for MFIs to stay: RBI
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: 
RBI
 has made it clear that microfinance institutions cannot allow borrowers' total monthly loan repayments to exceed 50% of their household income, rejecting an industry proposal to relax the cap by excluding principal repayments from the calculation.
The regulator, however, is open to reviewing the Rs 3 lakh annual household income ceiling for microfinance eligibility, depending on industry developments and its assessment of the need for a revision. "Excluding some loans from the calculation would defeat this purpose, tinker with the sanctity of the limit and understate household leverage," RBI deputy governor Shirish Chandra Murmu said.
Rejects industry proposal
Under RBI's 2022 regulatory framework, households with an annual income of up to Rs 3 lakh are eligible for microfinance loans from regulated lenders. Their total monthly loan repayments across lenders cannot exceed 50% of household income.
Known as the Fixed Obligation to Income Ratio (FOIR), the measure captures the proportion of a household's monthly income committed to servicing loans. For instance, if a household earns Rs 20,000 a month, its combined monthly repayments across loans cannot exceed Rs 10,000. Both principal and interest payments are included.
Microfinance lenders had sought a more accommodative interpretation that would exclude the principal component of certain loans and count only interest payments. This would have reduced the repayment burden recorded under FOIR and created room for lenders to extend additional credit without breaching the 50% ceiling.
Murmu said the objective of the cap was to prevent over-indebtedness, while ensuring that a reasonable share of household income remained available for essential consumption and other living expenses. He said 50% was already a liberal threshold given the limited financial cushion of low-income households and their vulnerability to economic shocks.
Citing a recent study, he said the average microfinance borrower spends 18.7% of monthly household income on loan repayments, while close to two-thirds goes towards consumption. NABARD's rural economic conditions and sentiments surveys showed a similar pattern, with consumption and other expenses accounting for roughly three-fourths of monthly household income.
"In such a scenario, an accommodative view on FOIR may be uncalled for," Murmu said, adding that the regulatory FOIR should be treated as a prudential maximum and not a target that every household has to meet.
On Rs 3 lakh annual household income threshold, Murmu said a review would be undertaken depending on RBI's assessment of the need for a revision and developments in the industry.

briefs.headline: Domestic demand, industry, earnings power growth in Q2
briefs.deck: Economists See GDP Expansion Of 7.5% Against 7.8% In Q1
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: On the back of resilient domestic demand, steady industrial activity and strong corporate earnings, the economy is projected to have sustained its growth momentum in the Sept quarter of the current financial year, with a TOI poll of 10 economists projecting real GDP expansion of 7.5% or more, following the 7.8% print recorded during April-June.
In its latest monetary policy review last month, RBI projected Sept quarter growth at 7.2%, with the finance ministry's monthly economic review pegging it at 7.35%. The National Statistical Office (NSO) is scheduled to release the official GDP data for the second quarter on Nov 30.
Based on its 54 high-frequency indicators across agriculture, industry and services, SBI expects Q2 growth to have been 7.8%, with nominal GDP expected to grow 11-11.5%, up from 10.3% in the June quarter.
DK Joshi of Crisil, too, estimated GDP to have grown at a similar pace during the quarter. "All the underlying data across sectors point to this, along with robust tax collection numbers."
Both IDFC First Bank chief economist Gaura Sengupta and Emkay Global economist Madhavi Arora expect Q2 growth to track around 8%, slightly higher than the June quarter. Sengupta noted that the momentum is led by manufacturing, with factory output growing 8.1% in Q2, alongside rising listed company profits due to strong sales outpacing input cost pressures. 
"Robust corporate tax and GST collections further corroborate the trend," she said.
DBS Bank senior economist Radhika Rao and HDFC Bank chief economist Sakshi Gupta projected Q2 growth at 7.7%, while CareEdge Ratings chief economist Rajani Sinha estimated it at 7.6%. Sinha pointed out that manufacturing drew strength from auto sales and core (non-oil, non-gold) exports, while front-loaded public capex, particularly steady state capex supported construction, despite a moderation in the centre's capex due to an adverse base.
"Services, however, presented a mixed bag as bank credit and services exports held firm, whereas air passenger traffic contracted deeper due to higher fares triggered by the West Asia conflict, alongside moderation in aviation turbine fuel (ATF) consumption and e-way bills," said Sinha.
ICRA chief economist Aditi Nayar and Bank of Baroda chief economist Madan Sabnavis project growth at 7.5% and 7.4%, respectively. "If Q2 growth exceeds our target, a larger repo rate hike of 50bps may be on the cards," said Nayar, amid inflation rising to 6.1%.
India Ratings chief economist DK Pant is the most conservative in his estimation, suggesting of at least 7% in Q2, with expectations of a softening urban consumption in coming months.
Economists pointed to the gaps in rural consumption, as evident in the surge in employment demand under the VB-G RAM G scheme alongside softer tractor and two-wheeler sales, with the brunt of a weak monsoon expected during the second half of financial year.

briefs.headline: Husband remits Rs 80L to seller for wife's property, she gets notice; what ITAT said
briefs.deck: According to the I-T department’s ‘Insight Portal’, the woman purchased an immovable property worth Rs 1.4 crore during the financial year that ended on March 31, 2016. The portal monitors high-value financial transactions to help detect instances of tax non-payment. The case was about Section 69 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, which deals with unexplained investments.
briefs.bodyText:
You buy a property, part of which is funded by your husband who stays abroad and remits money in the account of the seller. But the Income Tax Department treats it as unexplained investment and adds it to your taxable income. What do you do?
In one such case, a Mumbai woman’s taxable income was increased by Rs 80 lakh after the income-tax department questioned the amount paid towards the purchase of her residential property.
The Mumbai bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT) decided in her favour of a woman. Read on to know what happened:
What the case is about
According to the I-T department’s ‘Insight Portal’, the woman purchased an immovable property worth Rs 1.4 crore during the financial year that ended on March 31, 2016.
The portal monitors high-value financial transactions to help detect instances of tax non-payment. The case was about Section 69 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, which deals with unexplained investments.
The information originated from the sub-registrar’s office and was corroborated by data available in the tax deducted at source (TDS) statement relating to the transaction.
The woman had not originally filed her income-tax return, proceedings under Section 148A were initiated. 
She subsequently filed her return.
She explained that the investment was funded through proceeds from the sale of an earlier property and financial assistance from her husband who was residing and working in Dubai.
During the assessment, the Assessing Officer examined the registered sale deed, Form 26AS and the bank accounts of the woman and the seller. After accounting for TDS of Rs 1.40 lakh, the payment towards the property worked out to Rs 1,38,60,000.
The officer accepted payments totalling Rs 58.50 lakh. These included Rs 40 lakh paid on August 12, 2015, and Rs 18.50 lakh paid on August 26, 2015, which were reflected in the woman’s bank account and corresponded with entries in the seller’s account.
The remaining Rs 80 lakh was disputed. The woman said her husband had paid the amount directly to the seller through a Dubai exchange bureau in two installments of Rs 40 lakh each. The seller’s bank statement recorded two credits totalling Rs 80 lakh.
The Assessing Officer, however, held that this narration did not conclusively establish that the money had originated from the husband. He also noted the absence of remittance advice, exchange bureau records, transfer instructions and bank statements showing the debit from the husband’s account.
Consequently, Rs 80 lakh was treated as unexplained investment. A further Rs 10,000 was added as unexplained balance consideration, taking the total addition to Rs 80.10 lakh.
The Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) upheld the additions. She subsequently challenged the order in ITAT Mumbai and won relief
Why ITAT ruled in favour of the woman
Appearing before the ITAT, the woman argued that she had adequately explained the source of the entire Rs 1.4 crore investment and backed her claim with documentary evidence.
She provided a detailed reconciliation of the property’s purchase price, accounting for every component of the payment, including the Rs 80 lakh transferred directly by her husband to the seller.
To substantiate her case, she submitted the registered sale deed, the gift deed executed by her husband, his affidavit confirming the payments, bank statements and other relevant documents. These records, she maintained, established the movement of funds and demonstrated that the transaction was genuine.
The tribunal examined the documents collectively rather than treating the absence of the original remittance records as decisive. It noted that the purchase, the registered sale deed, the seller’s identity and receipt of the consideration were not disputed.
As the order stated: “There is no dispute regarding the purchase of the residential property by the assessee for a consideration of Rs.1,40,00,000/-.”
The tribunal also observed that neither the Assessing Officer nor the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals) had found the documents submitted by the woman to be false, fabricated or manipulated. The seller’s bank statement showed the disputed credits, while the husband’s affidavit confirmed that he had made the payments on her behalf. His identity documents and income-tax records were also placed before the tribunal.
It noted: “These evidences are not isolated documents but interconnected and corroborative pieces of evidence which collectively establish the source and movement of funds forming part of the property transaction.”
Another consideration was that the remittance records related to a transaction undertaken nearly ten years earlier. The tribunal found that the authorities had not conducted an inquiry with the seller or gathered adverse material from the bank to establish that the payments represented the woman’s own unaccounted money.
The order stated: “More importantly, neither of the authorities has recorded any finding that the documents furnished by the assessee are false, fabricated, manipulated or otherwise lacking in authenticity.”
The tribunal held that the explanation could not be rejected merely because one additional piece of corroborative evidence was unavailable when the other documents supported the transaction.
It concluded: “Suspicion, however strong, cannot substitute evidence, particularly when the surrounding facts and documentary material overwhelmingly support the explanation furnished by the assessee.”
It held that the woman had discharged the burden under Section 69 by establishing the contributor’s identity, financial capacity, source of funds and their use towards the property purchase. The tribunal accordingly directed the Assessing Officer to delete the entire Rs 80.10 lakh addition.
The appeal was allowed.

briefs.headline: Semiconductor boom may add 1 lakh jobs; senior engineers earn 6x IT salar
briefs.deck: Industry experts estimate over 1 lakh jobs in the next three years through the country’s efforts to build a semiconductor ecosystem of its own. Professionals with specialised skills, including process engineering, chip fabrication, chip design, systems engineering and product architecture, can earn four to six times the salaries of IT services professionals with similar experience. The difference…
briefs.bodyText:
India is betting big on the semiconductor industry to drive an important phase of its manufacturing leap and the focus is expected to create over one lakh jobs in the coming years.
Industry experts estimate over 1 lakh jobs in the next three years through the country’s efforts to build a semiconductor ecosystem of its own.
Hiring requirements in the semiconductor industry are also evolving, with recruitment extending beyond conventional chip-design roles.
Talent hunt in semiconductor industry
According to estimates by Boston Consulting Group (BCG), the country’s semiconductor workforce, currently pegged at 25,000, is expected to expand fourfold during this period.
Separately, a study by recruitment and staffing firm CIEL HR Services for ET indicates that companies in the sector could add around 67,500 jobs in the next 18 months.
Professionals with specialised skills, including process engineering, chip fabrication, chip design, systems engineering and product architecture, can earn four to six times the salaries of IT services professionals with similar experience. The difference is particularly pronounced at the mid-to-senior levels, Ankush Wadhera, partner and managing director at BCG told the financial daily.
“The supply of fit-for-role talent is not keeping pace with demand and, as a result, many players are looking outside India for senior talent,” said Wadhera.
The US and Southeast Asia have emerged as key destinations for companies seeking experienced professionals, with a significant share of the global talent pool comprising members of the Indian diaspora.
“Entry-level and mid-level talent can be easily trained, but it is senior talent that is in acute shortage in the country,” he said.
Specialists in focus
Companies are increasingly looking for specialists in process engineering, equipment maintenance, yield management, reliability engineering and advanced packaging, areas that involve high-value technical work.
A CIEL HR Services study estimates that India has around 1.5 lakh semiconductor professionals working across chip design, verification, engineering, testing and product development.
“About 43% of the workforce has more than 10 years of experience, while nearly three-fourths have over five years of experience,” said Aditya Narayan Mishra, CEO of CIEL HR Services.
A study of India’s semiconductor industry, found that Qualcomm has the highest number of current job openings in the sector. AMD ranks second, followed by Nvidia, Synopsys, Applied Materials, Infineon, Cadence and Micron.
“For years, India’s semiconductor workforce was almost entirely focused on design,” said Mishra. “Domestic fabrication and packaging units are now creating demand for roles in process engineering, equipment maintenance, yield management, reliability and advanced packaging, which until recently accounted for a negligible share of hiring.”
The shortage of skilled professionals remains acute. The study found that for every 100 engineers with expertise in microarchitecture, the semiconductor industry has 135 vacancies to fill.
Companies are looking beyond competitors in the semiconductor industry to meet their hiring requirements, increasingly tapping academic institutions and IT services firms for talent. Among the skills in greatest demand are physical design and timing closure, digital design and RTL (register transfer level) coding, and design verification.
Employers are also seeking professionals skilled in microarchitecture, emulation, formal verification, embedded systems and silicon bring-up. Proficiency in programming languages such as Python, C++, Verilog and SystemVerilog, which is used for hardware description and verification, is another sought-after skill.
For its analysis, CIEL examined semiconductor recruitment trends in India over the 12 months leading up to November 2026. The study covered approximately 45,000 job openings across more than 150 semiconductor companies.

stories.headline: 'Have to go with values': Akhtar on India's aggressive celebrations at Asia Cup final
stories.deck: Former Pakistan pacer Shoaib Akhtar praised India's aggressive approach after their one-wicket win over Pakistan in the 2026 Under-19 Asia Cup final but stressed the importance of respecting opponents. He claimed Pakistan were the stronger team throughout the tournament but failed to handle pressure in the final, while congratulating India on winning a record-extending ninth title.
stories.bodyText:
Former Pakistan fast bowler 
Shoaib Akhtar
 has reacted to India's aggressive celebrations after beating Pakistan in the Under-19 Asia Cup 2026 final.
While he appreciated the young Indian players' fighting spirit, he also stressed that cricketers should respect certain values while competing on the field.
India secured a thrilling one-wicket victory in Al Amerat on Saturday to win their record-extending ninth Under-19 Asia Cup title.
Chasing 338, India were under pressure before Mohit Ulva and Manal Chauhan put together a match-winning 57-run partnership from just 35 balls. Chauhan scored 47 off 32 deliveries, while Ulva remained unbeaten on 49 from 26 balls and hit the winning boundary on the final delivery.
Akhtar speaks on India's celebrations
The Indian players gave Pakistan's team an animated send-off after sealing the victory. Their celebrations sparked mixed reactions on social media, with some praising the aggression and others questioning the behaviour.
Akhtar said he shares a friendly relationship with several Indian players he faced during his career and believes respect should remain part of the game.
"We don't have to play cricket only, we also have to go with values. Even today, I say good things about Sachin Tendulkar. I still think he is the best batter in the world. 
Virender Sehwag and Sourav Ganguly, we all are good friends. We have never reacted against each other in such a way," Akhtar said after the game.
Akhtar makes big Pakistan claim
Despite Pakistan losing the final, Akhtar felt they had been the stronger team for most of the tournament. He believed they failed to deal with the pressure when the title was at stake, while India handled the crucial moments better.
"My message to India U19 boys: Do show the aggression. I liked it. But Pakistan was a far superior team, so much better throughout the tournament. Somehow, they couldn't handle the pressure. As always, India knows how to handle pressure in crunch moments," the former Pakistan pacer said.
He also congratulated India for their performance in the final.
"Congratulations to India. They played amazing cricket. India had the firepower, the belief and the players who could finish the game," he added.

stories.headline: 'There's a lot going on': Oz batter concerned about Khawaja's well-being
stories.deck: Matt Renshaw checked on Usman Khawaja amid the renewed Sandpapergate controversy after Pat Cummins called claims in Khawaja’s book “utter nonsense”. Renshaw said he wanted to ensure his friend was doing well but declined to comment on the 2018 scandal. David Warner and Chadd Sayers have also backed Khawaja, while Cricket Australia has shown no intention of reopening its investigation.
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Australian batter 
Matt Renshaw
 has expressed concern for 
Usman Khawaja
's well-being amid the renewed Sandpapergate controversy, revealing that he checked in on his friend after 
Pat Cummins
 publicly questioned some of the claims made in Khawaja's book, Sabr.
Cummins had described the claims as "utter nonsense" during a press conference on Friday, raising questions about his relationship with Khawaja.
Renshaw checks on Khawaja
Speaking after Australia's 135-run defeat to England in the second ODI in Adelaide, Renshaw said he wanted to make sure Khawaja was doing alright amid the growing controversy.
"I have spoken to Usman, just checking in on him," Renshaw said. "Haven't really spoken too much about what's going on, just sort of checking on him as a human — obviously there's a lot going on."
Renshaw, who scored 63 in the match, said he was not part of Australia's touring squad in South Africa in 2018 and therefore could not comment on what happened during the ball-tampering scandal.
"I wasn't there in Cape Town when it happened so I have got no idea what was going on, so tough for me to comment on that."
"But yeah, I think everyone as humans, obviously everything is going on, but I think the biggest thing is making sure everyone's OK."
Khawaja receives support
Khawaja has also received support from former teammate David Warner, who has backed him on multiple occasions.
Chadd Sayers, who was part of Australia's 2018 South Africa tour, also supported Khawaja on Sunday.
Despite fresh statements from Khawaja, Warner and Sayers, Cricket Australia has so far shown no willingness to reopen its investigation into the ball-tampering scandal.

stories.headline: Batting a worry as rookie pacers script rare triumph
stories.deck: The lack of conviction from the Indian batters almost takes the sheen away from the ODI series win ahead of the Tests
stories.bodyText:
India would have aspired for a white-ball sweep in New Zealand, but when they arrived on these shores nearly four weeks back, they would have known the enormity of the task that lay ahead of them. New Zealand in New Zealand are hard nuts to crack, whatever be the format, and while India fancied their chances, nothing was going to come easy. Or at least, that was the surmise.
That theory was exploded within the first week when the visitors charged to a winning 3-0 lead in the five-match Twenty20 International series. Those three victories were largely fashioned by the batting group, which should have come as no surprise to anyone because even in New Zealand, bowler-friendly New Zealand, the onus is decidedly on batter-loving surfaces in the shortest international version.

stories.headline: Arjun finds form, snaps Vachier-Lagrave’s winning run
stories.bodyText:
Arjun Erigaisi caught Maxime Vachier-Lagrave at the top of Group D on Saturday by handing the Frenchman his first Fast Classic defeat. Yet the Indian will go into Sunday’s two games against R. Vaishali needing to outscore both Vachier-Lagrave and Hans Niemann to stay in the title race at the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot in Budapest.
Magnus Carlsen’s challenge ended with two draws against Shakhriyar Mamedyarov. The World No. 1 is winless after eight games and can no longer finish first in Group C. Only the four group winners advance to the championship bracket.
Arjun began the day three points behind Vachier-Lagrave. He drew their first game with black, then won the return with white. Niemann beat Bibisara Assaubayeva before the Kazakh held him to a 96-move draw, leaving all three leaders on 13 points.
The opening blitz decides ties, and both Vachier-Lagrave and Niemann finished ahead of Arjun. Vachier-Lagrave faces Assaubayeva on Sunday, while Niemann plays Wesley So. So was the only player to win both games on Saturday, beating Vaishali twice to reach 10 points. Vaishali remains on four.
Carlsen, on seven points, faces Ian Nepomniachtchi in his final two games. Anish Giri took the Group C lead with a win and a draw against Abhimanyu Mishra. His 13 points put him two clear of Nepomniachtchi and overnight leader Haik Martirosyan.
Carlsen’s lead over Fabiano Caruana in the live classical ratings also narrowed, from 7.2 points at the start of play to 5.4. Caruana drew twice with his closest Group B rival, Liem Le, to remain unbeaten on 16 points, four clear of the Vietnamese.
R. Praggnanandhaa lost with black to Richard Rapport before drawing the return game to reach five points. Still seeking his first Fast Classic win, he faces Le while Caruana meets Vladislav Artemiev.
In Group A, Alireza Firouzja drew twice with Jan-Krzysztof Duda to retain the lead on 13 points. Duda and Jorden van Foreest, who meet on Sunday, are two points behind.
(The writer is in Budapest at the invitation of Total Chess).

briefs.headline: ‘Bowlers win you series!’: Gambhir’s message after India’s historic win in New Zealand
briefs.deck: India achieved a 3-1 ODI series victory against New Zealand, highlighted by strong bowling performances. The final match featured India's bowlers dismissing New Zealand for 187 runs while defending a total of 210. Gautam Gambhir praised the team's bowling depth after the win. Despite batting struggles, Shreyas Iyer acknowledged the players' resilience and commitment throughout the series.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India head coach 
Gautam Gambhir
 had a simple message after India's bowlers delivered a memorable series triumph in New Zealand: "Bowlers win you series!"
Gambhir congratulated the side following its 22-run victory over New Zealand in the fifth and final ODI at Bay Oval on Sunday, which sealed a 3-1 series win for the visitors. Taking to social media after the match, the head coach shared a photograph of the team celebrating with the trophy and wrote: "Bowlers win you series! Proud of our boys."
The victory was particularly significant as India registered only their third ODI series triumph in New Zealand, following their successes in 2009 and the 2018-19 season.
Defending a modest total of 210, India's bowlers produced a disciplined performance to dismiss the hosts for 187 in 48.1 overs. Left-arm pacer 
Arshdeep Singh
 led the attack with three wickets for 30 runs, while Axar Patel and Mohammed Siraj picked up two wickets each. Auqib Nabi, 
Yash Thakur
 and Naman Dhir also contributed with a wicket apiece.
New Zealand struggled to build momentum during the chase as India kept breaking partnerships. Dean Foxcroft top-scored with 31, while captain Mitchell Santner managed 24, but the hosts eventually fell 22 runs short.
Shreyas Iyer hails bowling depth and team character
India captain Shreyas Iyer also credited the bowling unit, highlighting how the players stood up despite challenging conditions and the pressure of defending a below-par total.
"Ecstatic. I think both the series T20 and ODI coming over here, we were provided with different conditions. 
The weather kept changing. Faced with a lot of challenges and coming out triumphs, I think it’s a great achievement. And today we had that certain kind of belief even though we didn’t get that many runs in batting. But still we were hoping that we can change the game at any point of time. And I’m glad that every individual thought in the same direction and we were able to execute that," Iyer said after the victory.
He added that the series had largely favoured bowlers rather than batters, praising the confidence and character of India's attack.
"Definitely if you see the whole series, it wasn’t a series for batsmen. The way the bowlers bowled, they stood up to the occasion and definitely were confident enough to see to it that they would get the team through irrespective of the conditions. I think that’s the mindset of all the players that we need and the character each and every individual possesses. It’s top notch," he said.
Iyer also acknowledged the challenge of managing changing combinations, with several players unavailable due to injuries and preparations for the Test assignments.
"Yes, absolutely. It becomes at some point of time becomes challenging for the players when there’s chopping and changing. They need to acclimatize to the condition and adapt as you mentioned earlier. But we didn’t want to give any excuse. We just wanted to live up to our expectations and every individual were just willing to come out here and give their best," he said.
India overcome batting collapse to seal series
Earlier, India were bowled out for 209 in 42.1 overs after being asked to bat first. Ishan Kishan and Axar were the leading contributors with 46 runs each, while Naman Dhir added a valuable 31 off 22 balls.
India had slumped to 34/3 after Rohit Sharma (7), Virat Kohli (5) and Ruturaj Gaikwad (18) departed cheaply. New Zealand captain Santner and Jacob Duffy claimed three wickets apiece to keep the visitors in check.
Despite the batting struggles, India's bowlers ensured the total was enough to secure the series. Iyer also thanked the Indian supporters who turned up in large numbers throughout the tour, praising the growing support for the sport.
"Off the field should be friendly, but on the field it’s like a war," he said, summing up the competitive spirit and mutual respect between the two sides.

briefs.headline: 'I should've never bought': Faf reveals why Kohli is his most expensive relationship
briefs.deck: Faf du Plessis revealed how Virat Kohli backed him unconditionally during his three-year stint as RCB captain from 2022 to 2024, despite the pressure of succeeding the Indian star. The two developed a close friendship, but Kohli also introduced du Plessis to luxury watches, prompting him to joke that Kohli was the “most expensive relationship” of his life.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: 
Faf du Plessis
 may have found an unwavering ally in 
Virat Kohli
 during his stint as Royal Challengers Bengaluru (RCB) captain, but the friendship came with an unexpectedly expensive side effect: a newfound obsession with luxury watches.
The former South Africa captain revealed that Kohli introduced him to the world of expensive timepieces, persuading him to buy watches he would never have considered otherwise.
"So I've said this to him, and I've said this publicly: the most expensive relationship of my life has been him. Because he's made me buy watches that I should have never, ever, ever bought," du Plessis said in a conversation with ESPNcricinfo.
He admitted that Kohli's influence had transformed him into a watch enthusiast, albeit one whose spending habits had become difficult to justify.
"Three years later, I've become the biggest watch guy. And now everyone is saying to me, how do you spend that much money on a watch?" he said.
Kohli had du Plessis' back during RCB captaincy
The friendship between the two developed during du Plessis' three-year stint as RCB captain from 2022 to 2024. Taking over the leadership from Kohli was never going to be straightforward, given the Indian batter's immense popularity and his deep connection with the franchise's supporters.
Du Plessis recalled feeling accepted by Kohli almost immediately after stepping into the role.
"There was always respect, but in an instant I felt accepted to step into the shoes," he said.
However, the pressure of succeeding Kohli was never far away. Du Plessis pointed out that even a single defeat could trigger demands from RCB supporters for the former captain to return to the leadership role.
"Let me tell you as a captain, if you lose two games, not even, if you lose one game for RCB, the whole of Bangalore and the whole of India want Virat Kohli to captain," he said.
"And it's not because they don't like you or me. They just want Virat Kohli to captain. So anything that doesn't happen that's a win comes down to: but Virat Kohli must be captain."
Du Plessis understood the expectations that came with leading one of the most popular franchises in Indian cricket. What made the challenge easier, however, was the support he received from Kohli, who remained an important part of the dressing room despite relinquishing the captaincy.
"Imagine if I didn't have that support, how I would have felt in those three years. It would have been the hardest time to deal with that," he said.
From opponents to close friends
The change in their respective roles also helped the two build a closer relationship. Du Plessis had previously been a captain while Kohli led India and RCB. With the South African now in charge and Kohli playing under him, their dynamic took on a different dimension.
"At that stage, I was a player coming from captaining someone and then not captaining the team anymore. So I had this fresh perspective that at least I was on the same level with him, now that he's a player," du Plessis explained.
He described Kohli's backing as unconditional and said their friendship came naturally, despite years of competing against each other on the cricket field.
"I had his support, more than unconditional support, from day one. He just had my back all the time," he said.
"I would say we had always played against each other, but instantly we felt like we had a very, very good friendship. There's no context here to it. There's no background. It was just, like, straight away."
For du Plessis, Kohli's support proved invaluable during his time as RCB captain, helping him navigate the expectations that came with succeeding one of the franchise's most celebrated players. The friendship, it seems, has endured beyond their time together at RCB, even if Kohli has left him with a considerably more expensive taste in watches.

briefs.headline: Worst ever! Rohit Sharma ends New Zealand series with unwanted career record
briefs.deck: During India's ODI series against New Zealand, Rohit Sharma faced uphill challenges, delivering a disappointing average of 7.50. With two ducks contributing to his low scores over four innings, his best effort registered at only 23 runs. Nonetheless, India clinched a 22-run victory in the last ODI, finishing the series 3-1.
briefs.bodyText:
Rohit Sharma
 endured a forgettable outing in India's ODI series against New Zealand, registering the lowest batting average of his career in a bilateral ODI series as an opener. The former India captain managed just 30 runs in five matches and four innings, averaging a mere 7.50.
Rohit's scores in the series read 0, 23, 0 and 7, with two ducks highlighting his struggles against the New Zealand bowling attack. His latest failure came in the fifth and final ODI at the Bay Oval on Sunday, when he was dismissed for seven after flicking a length delivery straight to mid-wicket off Matthew Fisher.
The series turned out to be a particularly disappointing one for Rohit, who has been one of India's most prolific ODI batters. His struggles were also reflected in his overall record across countries, with New Zealand now among the places where he has his lowest ODI batting averages.
Rohit Sharma's ODI batting average by country
Rohit averages 19.69 in South Africa, his lowest in any country, followed by 29.00 in Pakistan and 29.18 in New Zealand. His other country-wise averages include 31.13 in Sri Lanka, 34.08 in Bangladesh, 48.09 in the West Indies, 56.10 in India, 56.66 in Australia, 59.83 in Zimbabwe, 62.12 in the UAE and 64.12 in England.
India, meanwhile, signed off from the series with a 22-run victory in the final ODI, defending a modest total of 209 to secure a 3-1 series win. The triumph also ended New Zealand's seven-year unbeaten run in home ODI series and gave 
Gautam Gambhir
 his first ODI series victory overseas as India's head coach.
The bowlers were instrumental in the win, with 
Arshdeep Singh
 leading the charge with figures of 3/30. Mohammed Siraj and Axar Patel claimed two wickets apiece as New Zealand were bowled out for 187 in 48.1 overs.
India's batting, however, had once again left plenty to be desired. Rohit and Virat Kohli fell for single-digit scores, while Axar Patel and Ishan Kishan top-scored with 46 each. Contributions from the lower order, particularly a 26-run last-wicket stand between Siraj and Arshdeep, proved crucial in taking India past 200.
For Rohit, though, the series will be remembered for an unwanted personal milestone, with his average of 7.50 marking the lowest he has recorded in an ODI series as an opener.

briefs.headline: Record alert! Kagiso Rabada surpasses Allan Donald in SA’s all-time wicket tally
briefs.deck: Kagiso Rabada reached a remarkable career milestone by exceeding Allan Donald's wicket record, bagging five wickets to elevate his total to 606 in international cricket. Although Bangladesh faced an early struggle, they mounted a strong comeback driven by an incredible 206-run partnership between Towhid Hridoy and Litton Das, concluding the day at 327 for 6 and revitalising their innings.
briefs.bodyText:
Kagiso Rabada
 added another milestone to his illustrious career on Sunday, surpassing legendary fast bowler 
Allan Donald
 to become South Africa’s fourth-highest wicket-taker in international cricket. However, the landmark moment was followed by a spirited Bangladesh fightback on the opening day of the first Test.
Rabada claimed five wickets for 51 runs to take his international tally across Tests, ODIs and T20Is to 606, moving past Donald's 602. Shaun Pollock leads the South African charts with 823 wickets, followed by Dale Steyn (697) and Makhaya Ntini (661).
The 31-year-old also registered his 18th five-wicket haul in Test cricket, drawing level with Ntini for joint-third place on South Africa's all-time list. Donald is second with 20 five-fors, while Steyn leads the standings with 26.
Rabada strikes early as Bangladesh lose top order
Rabada made an immediate impact, striking twice in the opening exchanges as Bangladesh endured a difficult start. Debutant Mahfijul Islam fell for a first-ball duck, while Mominul Haque also departed without scoring.
The fast bowler then produced a superb delivery to dismiss Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto, leaving the visitors reeling at 22/3.
Tanzid Hasan and Towhid Hridoy attempted to stabilise the innings with a valuable partnership. Tanzid scored 67 before Rabada returned after lunch to remove him and Mushfiqur Rahim in quick succession, completing his five-wicket haul.
Bangladesh were struggling at 121/5, but the contest took a dramatic turn thereafter.
Hridoy, Litton script remarkable recovery
Hridoy found an able partner in Litton Das as the duo turned the innings around with an unbroken sixth-wicket stand of 206 runs, the highest partnership by a Bangladesh pair against South Africa in their Test encounters.
Hridoy produced a magnificent 137 off 208 deliveries, registering his maiden Test century against South Africa. He became only the second Bangladesh batter to score a Test hundred against the Proteas after Mahmudul Hasan Joy in 2022.
Litton, meanwhile, remained unbeaten on 92 as Bangladesh finished the opening day at 327/6, recovering from a precarious position to take control of the innings.

briefs.headline: Archery nationals: Kumkum, Chikitha in line for gold medals
briefs.bodyText:
Asian Games gold medallists Kumkum Mohod and Chikitha Taniparthi proved their mettle to reach the recurve and compound women’s individual title clashes respectively in the National archery championships at the Parade Ground here on Sunday.
Both Kumkum and Chikitha secured their maiden National individual medals in elimination stage.
Kumkum toppled strong opponents, including Ridhi Phor, Simranjeet Kaur and Sharvari Shende, to enter the final. She will meet Olympian and her Asiad women’s team gold medal winning team-mate Ankita Bhakat, who beat her Jharkhand pal Komalika Bari, in the final.
Chikitha shot consistently good scores and held her nerve in a tense semifinal match against World Cup Stage medallist Madhura Dhamangaonkar. She found issues with her footing and trailed 28-30 in the first end before a cheeky remark from Madhura irked her.
Chikitha bounced back with a firm resolve to shoot four perfect consecutive rounds and record a 148-147 victory. Madhura, leading by one point after the penultimate end, slipped in the final.
“After losing two points, I told myself to focus on giving my best in the remaining ends. I just followed the process which brought me success at the Asian Games,” said Chikitha, who would meet another first-timer, Madhuravarshini Muruganantham, in the summit clash.
Madhuravarshini, barring her wind-affected pre-quarterfinal match (136-135) against Tamil Nadu team-mate S. Deekshita, gave a series of fine performances to make a bit of history by becoming the first from her state to ensure a podium finish.
“It’s a breakthrough performance. I was not expecting anything as I made a lot of changes, including a change of place (to SAI, Sonepat) for training,” said Madhuravarshini.
The experienced Rajat Chauhan and the promising Priyansh will face off in the compound men’s final.
Olympian B. Dhiraj will take on a lesser-known Dhruv Bagga in the recurve men’s gold medal match.

briefs.headline: Shahrukh Khan sheds light on Dinesh Karthik’s influence on him and Tamil Nadu’s IPL generation
briefs.deck: Shahrukh, after a disappointing last season, has started out on a positive note this time around
briefs.bodyText:
Shahrukh Khan (46 n.o., 30b, 5x4, 2x6) — who was dropped from the Tamil Nadu squad midway through the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy (SMAT) last season — helped his team manage a mid-innings wobble and score a competitive 172 for seven against Railways in its season opener this time.
Tamil Nadu eventually pipped Railways by six runs at the Daly College ground here on Saturday.
Coming in at 83 for three in 11.3 overs, Shahrukh revealed that Dinesh Karthik’s advice had influenced his approach. Karthik had interacted with the players during a practice session ahead of the tournament.
“Dinesh told me that I could hit at any time and take on the bowlers whenever I wanted. But the most important thing was to take the team through a tough situation. When I came in, it wasn’t easy because we had lost two quick wickets. In terms of mindset, he has really helped me with the way he spoke to me during practice. His thoughts and words have always had a big influence on me. I think I’ve produced my best for Tamil Nadu under his captaincy,” he said.
He credited Karthik with laying the foundation for Tamil Nadu’s IPL generation.
“Five or six years ago, we had 10-12 players from Tamil Nadu playing in the IPL. The credit goes to him because we came in as youngsters and he really taught us how to play T20 cricket, how to go about things as a team, and how to win,” he said.
Shahrukh also acknowledged coach Yo Mahesh’s role in helping him understand his responsibility.
“Yomi has also been having conversations with me over the last 20 days. Even during the Ranji Trophy, he called and spoke to me about how things were going and what he expected from me. A sense of calmness is really important. I calculated things well as the innings progressed,” he said.

briefs.headline: ‘He takes pressure off’: Lakshya on Sehwag’s impact in India’s Asia Cup triumph
briefs.deck: Lakshya Raichandani commended Aaryavir Sehwag for his exceptional play during the Under-19 Asia Cup. Sehwag's impressive scoring led the team to triumph, showcasing a remarkable recovery following a previous defeat to Pakistan. Raichandani emphasised the critical role of a reliable batter in successful run chases, underscoring the team's resilience and the valuable lessons they learned from their…
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India Under-19 captain Lakshya Raichandani has credited Aaryavir Sehwag’s attacking batting for making life easier for his teammates, saying the opener’s ability to put opposition bowlers under pressure takes the burden off the batter at the other end.
Aaryavir was one of the standout performers in India's Under-19 Asia Cup title-winning campaign, finishing as the tournament's leading run-scorer with 361 runs in five innings. His consistent performances also earned him the player-of-the-tournament award.
Praising the opener's contribution, Raichandani described him as both a fine batter and a wonderful human being, while explaining how his approach changes the dynamics of an innings.
"Yeah, he's a really good batter (Aaryavir) and a wonderful human being. When he bats, it takes some pressure off the batter at the other end because of the way he plays. It also makes batting easier on the track, as he puts the opposition bowlers under pressure and forces them to release that pressure by offering loose deliveries to the other batter," Raichandani said.
‘We never stopped believing’: India bounce back against Pakistan
India's triumph was particularly special as they overcame a group-stage defeat to arch-rivals Pakistan before beating them by one wicket in a nail-biting final in Al Amerat, Oman, on Saturday.
Reflecting on his experience of leading the side to the title, Raichandani said the team developed a strong understanding throughout the campaign.
"It was a pretty good experience. We had a really good rapport with each other, and it was a great experience overall. I'm proud of the guys and really privileged to be leading this team," he said.
The captain also explained the team's straightforward batting approach, stressing the importance of making the most of the powerplay and having at least one set batter stay until the end.
"My approach was simple. If one batter gets set at one end and takes the innings deep, it makes the chase much easier. Our approach was straightforward, and getting a good start in the powerplay was important.
"Hopefully, we managed to provide that start, and the plan after that was for one of the set batters to stay till the end," the skipper said.
Raichandani admitted the group-stage loss to Pakistan provided important lessons, but insisted that the team's belief in its approach never wavered.
"In the first match, our plan was quite simple. After losing, we realised the areas where we could improve and where we could have done better. That was one important takeaway. Overall, though, our plan remained the same, and we believed in our approach," he said.
"We never stopped believing. We were quite optimistic, and we continued to believe in the team till the very end."
